blocks.text: Jerusalem was both a royal center and a center of worship, joining kingship, temple life, pilgrimage, judgment, and hope for restored worship in one place. This background gives weight to the vision in which instruction goes out from Zion and the nations gather at Jehovah’s house: Jerusalem is presented as the focal point of divine teaching and worship amid the pressures surrounding it.

Jerusalem’s history extends from a Jebusite city to the Davidic capital and temple center, and later to a focal point of exile, return, and messianic expectation. Isaiah’s vision of peoples streaming there therefore places the city within a much larger story of rule, worship, loss, restoration, and hope.

Isaiah 2:2-4 closely parallels Micah 4:1-3 in its language about Zion, divine instruction, judgment between nations, and weapons remade as agricultural tools. The close verbal relationship is clear, although how the two prophetic passages are historically related remains disputed.

The opening vision belongs to Isaiah’s broader, complex portrayal of the nations. Judah, Israel, and foreign peoples all come under judgment; empires may serve as instruments yet remain accountable themselves; and the nations can also be pictured learning, worshiping, and sharing in restoration. Isaiah 2:1-5 emphasizes this hopeful side as many peoples seek Jehovah’s instruction and accept his adjudication.

The Great Isaiah Scroll preserves an almost complete witness to Isaiah’s sixty-six chapters. It broadly aligns with the Masoretic tradition while containing thousands of differences in spelling and substance. Other Isaiah manuscripts and interpretive writings found at Qumran likewise reflect the book’s active transmission and interpretation, though the significance of particular differences remains a matter of study.
